body: Nodes added via editable children are not part of the instance. If their owner were pointing to the instance, they wouldn't be saved in the parent scene, and since you can't modify an instance from another scene, not saved at all.

I don't think I understand that.
As far as I can tell, scene instances represent a "copy" of the scene that allows editing per-instance data of the original scene "blueprint", so the data is saved somewhere per instance. Wouldn't that also be – at least close to – where the data for the added Node, or really any "edited child" should be saved?
> Nodes added via editable children are not part of the instance.

"Editable children" sounds like it makes the children of the scene instance we clicked on editable, and adding a node into the list of the other children of that instance should add it as a child of that instance, which it did – or at least it was part part of the children of the scene instance's root node at runtime.
Shouldn't it just save the override of its children somewhere, as it would with the other overridden data of its children? Why would the node not be saved if the owner doesn't match the root? The owner of any other node in the instance is the instance's scene's root, not the root of the scene, but their overrides are still saved, somewhere.

Also, isn't "editable children" meant to allow modifying an instance – specifically, its children, as the properties are modifiable in the inspector already – from another scene?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/026915c9-47cc-4c89-a1f7-71cb7948e5ef)

All white nodes here are owned by the Root scene. Instance's owner is also Root, but it's a separate scene with its own children (the EditableChild shown in yellow). Changes to EditableChild are not part of Instance scene, but they are stored in Root scene. Also the AdoptedChild node is part of Root, it's only placed under Instance. You can toggle editable children without affecting that node.

You can't modify Instance scene itself from within Root scene. All changes are regarded as overrides and stored in Root. You also can't change the Instance's nodes; you can only override their properties, but you can't delete them or change their type.

> All white nodes here are owned by the Root scene. Instance's owner is also Root, but it's a separate scene with its own children (the EditableChild shown in yellow).

Instance is an instantiation of the Scene scene (I'll assume that's the scene's name to differentiate them) and that instance is part of the Root scene. 
Being an instance of a scene allows Instance to have different data than the Scene scene originally intended. Got that.

> Changes to EditableChild are not part of Instance scene, but they are stored in Root scene. Also the AdoptedChild node is part of Root [...]

I can also see why this works the way it does. One can hardly apply changes to some instance of the Scene scene to the scene itself whenever or wherever they happen, so storing the overrides in the Root scene, where they are defined, makes perfect sense, whether these changes be to properties or the children's properties or to the list of children, as is the case with adding the new child AdoptedChild to the instance Instance (not to the Scene scene).
Changes to Instance, EditableChild, and AdoptedChild are stored in Root. Got that, too.

> [...] , it's only placed under Instance.

This is where I'm not following. Why is it placed there if it doesn't belong there? Or rather, why is it *only* placed there instead of making it part of that instance? 

> You can't modify Instance scene itself from within Root scene. All changes are regarded as overrides and stored in Root. 

Yes, but you can modify an instance of a scene, which should include its children, and then you could store those along the "instance overrides" in Root.

>You also can't change the Instance's nodes; you can only override their properties, but you can't delete them or change their type.

The original Scene scene may change in a way that requires certain nodes or them to be a certain type, so I can see why that'd not be possible, but adding nodes shouldn't have that problem, and, as far as I can tell, the AdoptedChild becomes a child of Instance for most intents and purposes, except that it starts with Root as owner, as opposed to the other children of Instance (and maybe some other differences I couldn't tell).

I solved my issue by just copying the siblings owner on ready, but having two siblings start out referring to different owners seems wrong.

If you add 2 Instance nodes and add a child to one of them, should it be applied to the base scene (i.e. appear in all instances), or only in that instance?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c8a4b575-5f9b-4007-a9ad-1ffb99510738)
As is the case with overriding properties, changes to an instance should only affect the instance itself while changes to a scene should affect all instances.

Yes, so the same as overrides, the modification is stored in the root scene, so the node is owned by the root scene. That's just how owner system works. You can't have `owner` point to the Instance and get saved as part of the Root scene.

In either case, it's expected behavior and I explained as much as I could.
If you feel something should be changed, open a [proposal/discussion](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals).

I realize that I was under a misconception about the role of owner. The specific scenario described in the title wouldn't be expected behavior, as the current behavior regarding the adopted child is as per the definition, so the issue as phrased in the title can be closed.

But the body of the issue is about the discrepancy between sibling nodes in general and by extension, since the title's scenario  turned out to be the expected version, about why the owner is *not* the root node of the scene that it was edited in *only* when it's an edited child.

So I'd say that the root of this issue still persists.
Editable children still belong to their original scene, enabling this flag only makes them visible in the scene dock.

Okay, so creating a node in a scene creates an ownership relation between the scene and the node, which decides which scene stores its overrides, but overriding a node does not create that ownership relation, yet the override of an editable child is still stored in the scene because its owner has itself an owner, which is then taken as the node that stores it. At least, I assume that's the reason. 

Can't say I find it very intuitive, but I don't want to annoy you further with this discussion. Now that I know about this distinction I can just keep it in mind, and I've already solved the original (non-)issue by using a different approach, anyway. 

Thanks for your time!
